name: TeamStarWolf - macOS & Linux Attacks
description: Curated practitioner view, not an official MITRE mapping. Scores are membership tiers (core=100, supporting=55), not severity, confidence, incident frequency, or a coverage guarantee. Technique IDs and tactic assignments are validated against the bundled Enterprise ATT&CK 19.2 dataset, with official 16.1 retained as the original provenance baseline; tactic slugs follow 19.2. Selected Unix execution, persistence, credential access, privilege abuse, remote access, and follow-on behavior. A technique need only apply to one of macOS or Linux, not both; per-row platform metadata narrows its scope. The selection is not a complete operating-system matrix.

techniques.comment: Unix Shell. Core: Unix shells provide execution on Linux and macOS; correlate interpreter activity with user and process context.
AppleScript. Core: AppleScript can automate macOS applications during intrusion; automation alone is not malicious.
Launch Agent. Core: Launch agents can arrange recurring execution in macOS user sessions.

Systemd Service. Core: Linux systemd service changes can establish persistent execution with the service account's privileges.

Plist File Modification. Core: macOS property-list changes can redirect application or service behavior for persistence.
SSH Authorized Keys. Core: Unauthorized SSH keys can preserve access under an existing Unix account.
SSH Authorized Keys. Core: Unauthorized SSH keys can preserve access under an existing Unix account.
Setuid and Setgid. Core: Abuse of setuid or setgid behavior can cross Unix privilege boundaries.
Sudo and Sudo Caching. Core: Sudo policy or cached authorization can be abused to run commands with elevated privileges.
TCC Manipulation. Core: Manipulating macOS privacy-consent controls can bypass access restrictions on protected resources.
Keychain. Core: macOS Keychain access can expose credentials; evaluate caller identity and authorization.
/etc/passwd and /etc/shadow. Core: Linux password-database access can expose password hashes for subsequent credential attacks.
Private Keys. Core: Exposed private keys can enable access to Unix hosts or other services.
Gatekeeper Bypass. Core: Bypassing Gatekeeper weakens macOS execution-trust checks.
Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification. Core: Unix permission changes can make files accessible or executable outside their intended access model.
SSH. Core: SSH can carry authenticated movement between systems; normal administration needs a baseline.
Clear Linux or Mac System Logs. Core: Clearing Linux or macOS system logs can remove evidence of an intrusion.
Clear Command History. Core: Clearing command history can conceal interactive activity on a Unix host.
Exploit Public-Facing Application. Supporting: A vulnerable exposed application can provide entry to a Linux or macOS system.
Local Accounts. Supporting: Abused local accounts can supply a foothold or continued access without new malware.

Malicious File. Supporting: A user may execute an untrusted file; assess provenance and subsequent behavior.
Exploitation for Privilege Escalation. Supporting: A local software vulnerability can enable privilege escalation beyond the compromised account.
Credentials In Files. Supporting: Configuration and other local files may expose reusable credentials.
Disable or Modify Tools. Supporting: Disabling host security tools can reduce visibility before further activity.
System Information Discovery. Supporting: System inventory can help an intruder choose compatible tooling and targets.
File and Directory Discovery. Supporting: File enumeration can identify configuration, credentials, or data worth collecting.
Process Discovery. Supporting: Process enumeration can reveal running applications and defensive services.
System Network Configuration Discovery. Supporting: Network configuration can reveal local connectivity and possible next systems.
Local Account. Supporting: Local account discovery can identify useful identities and privilege boundaries.
Data from Local System. Supporting: Local files can become collection targets after access is obtained.
Ingress Tool Transfer. Supporting: Transferring tools onto a host can support follow-on execution.
Web Protocols. Supporting: Web protocols may carry command-and-control traffic; protocol use alone is not evidence of compromise.
Exfiltration Over C2 Channel. Supporting: An established command-and-control channel may also carry stolen data.
Data Encrypted for Impact. Supporting: Encryption can deny access to data on compromised Linux or macOS systems.
Resource Hijacking. Supporting: Unauthorized resource use can consume Unix-host compute or increase operating costs.

metadata.name: selection_rule
metadata.value: Core: platform-focused execution, persistence, trust-control abuse, credentials and SSH behaviors. Supporting: selected cross-platform intrusion behaviors relevant to Linux or macOS. Library hardening guidance supplies context, not an official hardening-to-ATT&CK crosswalk.

metadata.name: score_meaning
metadata.value: 100=core; 55=supporting. Membership only, not severity, prevalence, confidence, or measured defensive coverage.

metadata.name: tactic_policy
metadata.value: Display each selected technique under all of its official 19.2 tactics, verified to match the bundled snapshot. Display expansion does not assert a scenario uses every tactic or requires every step. The app may translate retired IDs for its newer live matrix.

metadata.name: validation_source
metadata.value: Official Enterprise ATT&CK 16.1 (original provenance baseline) and src/assets/data/enterprise-attack.json (collection version 19.2). v19 replaced the Defense Evasion tactic with Stealth and Defense Impairment, and retired the T1562 family in favour of T1685/T1686; technique IDs and tactic slugs follow the bundled 19.2 dataset.
